passages.text: Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is a model for understanding the motivations for human behavior. These include physiological needs, safety, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. The psychologist Abraham Maslow created this model. It maps different motivations onto a five-level pyramid, with each level representing a different human need. Maslow also felt that fulfillment in life results from being able to meet the needs in all five levels. He believed that people could not focus on the needs higher up the pyramid until they had mostly obtained the needs in the lower levels. Keep reading to learn more about Maslow’s hierarchy of needs and its applications, as well as what happens when the needs are unmet and criticisms of the theory. Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is a psychological theory about what drives human behavior and what makes humans feel fulfilled. It represents five key human needs that people must meet in order to achieve well-being. In an article in the journal Business Horizons, McDermid asserts that Maslow’s theory of motivation provides better insight (than classic economic theory) into the dynamics underlying human behaviour. More specifically, he states, "the hierarchy of needs is arranged in a pyramid of five levels, from basic physiological drives at the bottom to the desire for self-realisation, the highest expression of the human spirit, at the apex".[25] The most fundamental four layers of the pyramid contain what Maslow called "deficiency needs" or "d-needs": esteem, friendship and love, security, and physical needs. If these "deficiency needs" are not met – except for the most fundamental (physiological) need – there may not be a physical indication, but the individual will feel anxious and tense. passages.text: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is an attempt to describe what motivates us humans to do what we do or to behave in certain ways. Maslow published his description in 1943, and since then, it has been used in a number of fields, including psychology and management theory. Abraham Maslow was the oldest child of a Jewish family who immigrated from Kyiv, Ukraine in the early 1900s. He studied psychology and earned his PhD from the University of Wisconsin in 1934. After that, he moved back to his hometown of Brooklyn, New York, so he could teach at Brooklyn College. While there, he met many European intellectuals who had immigrated to the U.S. during the lead up to World War II. His ideas and thinking were thus influenced by famous psychiatrists and psychoanalysts like Alfred Adler, Erich Fromm, and Karen Horney.Â Brief description of what it means? Their form varies and need not be creative. Maslow argued that survival needs must be satisfied before the individual can satisfy the higher needs. The higher up the hierarchy, the more difficult it is to satisfy the needs associated with that stage, because of the interpersonal and environmental barriers that inevitably frustrate us. Maslow described this shift as gradual, not sudden. Higher needs become increasingly psychological and long-term rather than physiological and short-term, as in the lower survival-related needs. At once other (and “higher”) needs emerge and these, rather than physiological hungers, dominate the organism. passages.text: of Maslow’s hierarchy? The standard five levels are physiological needs, safety needs, love and belonging, esteem, and self-actualization. The first levels focus more directly on survival, security, and social needs, while self-actualization concerns growth and fuller development of capacities. Later versions and discussions sometimes include additional needs, but the five-level form remains the best-known version. Do lower needs have to be fully satisfied before higher needs matter? No. That is a common overstatement of the theory. Maslow wrote about relative and partial satisfaction, and he acknowledged exceptions. Severe deprivation may make some basic needs especially powerful, but people can still value relationships, dignity, purpose, creativity, or moral commitments while lower needs remain imperfectly met. Did Maslow create the famous pyramid? No. Historical research indicates that the iconic pyramid was created later as Maslow’s ideas moved into management education and textbooks. The shape is a memorable teaching device, but it encourages a more rigid interpretation than Maslow’s original writings require. What evidence supports or challenges the hierarchy? Evidence supports the importance of multiple kinds of needs and shows that need fulfillment relates to well-being. The weaker part is the claim of a strict, universal order. This is what we mean by saying that the basic human needs are organized into a hierarchy of relative prepotency. Keep in mind that Maslow’s hierarchy of needs doesn’t follow a strict linear progression. Individuals can feel various needs at the same time. They may also shift between levels as circumstances change. Maslow refined this idea over several decades (Maslow, 1943, 1962, 1987). Maslow (1987) later softened his own claim. He wrote that the order “is not nearly as rigid” (p. 68) as he had implied earlier, and that it could flex with circumstances or individual differences. For example, some people find self-esteem more urgent than love. Others place creative fulfilment above even their most basic needs. Maslow (1987) also stressed that behaviour is rarely driven by one need alone. He noted that “any behavior tends to be determined by several or all of the basic needs simultaneously rather than by only one of them” (p. 71). What Are the Different Types of Needs? Someone dealing with poverty, displacement, illness, discrimination, or instability is not a “lower-level person.” Their circumstances may create urgent needs that deserve attention. Likewise, wealth does not automatically produce belonging, esteem, or self-actualization. Resources can reduce some forms of deprivation without resolving every social, emotional, or growth-related concern. Recognize that multiple needs may matter simultaneously A realistic use of the model allows several needs to be active at once. A parent may seek stable housing, emotional closeness, professional competence, and meaningful contribution in the same month. A student may need sleep, safety, friendship, confidence, and intellectual challenge in the same week. The practical value of Maslow’s hierarchy is therefore not in forcing experience into five separate boxes. It is in noticing that motivation changes when different human needs become more or less urgent, and that context can reshape those priorities quickly. Maslow proposed that more basic needs tend to become especially powerful when deprived, but he did not describe human motivation as a perfectly rigid sequence. Modern research supports the importance of multiple needs while challenging a universal fixed hierarchy. What Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs Proposes Human needs as motivational influences Abraham Maslow introduced his theory in the 1943 paper A Theory of Human Motivation. Instead of explaining behavior through one drive, one reward system, or one external force, he proposed that human motivation reflects several kinds of needs. When an important need is strongly deprived, it may organize attention and behavior around restoring what is missing. That does not mean every action has a single hidden need behind it. A person can go to work partly for income, partly for security, partly for belonging, partly for recognition, and partly because the work expresses a valued ability. The hierarchy is better understood as a model of changing motivational priority than as a one-cause explanation for behavior. passages.text: Maslow's hierarchy of needs | Part of a series on | | Psychology | |---| | Part of a series on | | Sociology | |---| Maslow's hierarchy of needs is a conceptualization of the needs (or goals) that motivate human behaviour, which was proposed in 1943 by the American psychologist Abraham Maslow.[1][2] According to Maslow's original formulation, there are five sets of basic needs that are related to each other in a hierarchy of prepotency (or strength). Typically, the hierarchy is depicted in the form of a pyramid although Maslow himself was not responsible for the iconic diagram.[3] The pyramid begins at the bottom with physiological needs (the most prepotent of all) and culminates at the top with self-actualization needs. In his later writings, Maslow added a sixth level of "meta-needs" and metamotivation.[4][5] The hierarchy of needs developed by Abraham Maslow is one of his most enduring contributions to psychology.[6] The hierarchy of needs remains a popular framework and tool in higher education,[7][8] business and management training,[9] sociology research, healthcare,[10][11] counselling[12] and social work.[13] Although widely used and researched, the hierarchy of needs has been criticized for its lack of conclusive supporting evidence and its validity remains contested.[14][15][16][17] Historical

One of the earliest, in 1962, shows a more dynamic hierarchy in terms of 'waves' of different needs overlapping at the same time.[28] As illustrated, the peak of an earlier main set of needs must be passed before the next 'higher' need can begin to assume a dominant role. Other schematic illustrations of the hierarchy use overlapping triangles to depict the interaction of the different needs. One such updated hierarchy proposes that self-actualization is removed from its privileged place atop the pyramid because it is largely subsumed within status (esteem) and mating-related motives in the new framework.[29] Needs [edit] Physiological needs [edit] Physiological needs are the base of the hierarchy. These needs are the biological component for human survival. According to Maslow's hierarchy of needs, physiological needs are factored into internal motivation. According to Maslow's theory, humans are compelled to satisfy physiological needs first to pursue higher levels of intrinsic satisfaction.[1] To advance to higher-level needs in Maslow's hierarchy, physiological needs must be met first. This means that if a person is struggling to meet their physiological needs, they are unwilling to seek safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization on their own.

External praise may feel rewarding, but recognition without real competence can be fragile. Conversely, someone may develop skill and self-respect even when public recognition is limited. The model therefore points to both social and internal dimensions of esteem. Self-actualization Self-actualization refers to developing and expressing one’s capacities more fully. Maslow described it as a growth-oriented concern rather than simply repairing a deficit. It may involve creativity, purpose, meaningful work, honesty about one’s capacities, or a deeper commitment to what a person is capable of becoming. It is not a certificate of psychological superiority. Nor does reaching a meaningful period of growth mean lower-level concerns disappear. A person can be deeply engaged in creative work and still need rest, security, connection, and respect. How Maslow Thought the Hierarchy Worked Prepotency of needs Maslow’s central idea was not merely that five needs exist. He proposed that they differ in relative priority. The self-actualization teaching is not generalizable Another criticism of the concept of self-actualization is that Maslow largely based his ideas on the biographies of notable historical figures, most of whom were educated white men. As such, the traits he observed in these successful individuals may not apply to all people. Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is a theory about what motivates and fulfills humans. The theory includes five needs, each of which forms one section on a pyramid. At the foundation of the pyramid are physiological and safety needs. In the middle, there are social needs, such as love and belonging. At the top are esteem and self-actualization. People have applied the hierarchy in a range of ways, including in education, child development, and healthcare.
